description: At least nine states allow recovery for the wrongful death of a pre-viable baby. Alabama's Hamilton vs. Scott decision and what it could mean for Georgia.
shortAnswer: On February 17, 2012, the Alabama Supreme Court recognized that a family who loses an unborn child has the right to sue when their baby dies due to medical negligence, whether or not the child had reached the point of viability. At least nine states allow recovery of damages for the wrongful death (or injury) of a pre-viable baby.

faq.q: Can parents in Georgia recover for the wrongful death of an unborn child?
faq.a: Georgia and Mississippi permit recovery for the wrongful death (or injury) of an unborn child if the mother has felt the baby move inside the womb prior to the time of the injury. This movement is referred to as "quickening."

faq.q: How early in pregnancy can quickening occur, and how is it proved?
faq.a: Quickening occurs earlier than viability. Courts in Georgia have recognized that quickening can occur as early as 10 weeks into a pregnancy. One way to prove that quickening has occurred is to produce medical documentation that the mother felt the baby move prior to the injury or death.

faq.q: What does "viability" mean for an unborn baby?
faq.a: Viability refers to the ability of the baby to survive outside the womb, even if only in an incubator.

faq.q: Should Georgia courts follow the Hamilton vs. Scott decision?
faq.a: Georgia courts would do well to look to the Hamilton vs. Scott decision as persuasive authority. I believe Georgia law should recognize a cause of action for wrongful death or injury to an unborn child at any point in a pregnancy when the death or injury flows from the negligence of a person other than a family member.
